name: Yaki Udon
steps: Check the udon pack is eggless and the soy sauce contains no animal-derived ingredients. Pat the tofu dry and cut into 2 cm cubes. Cut cabbage into bite-size pieces, carrot into thin sticks, onion into thin slices and mushrooms into slices. Finely chop ginger. Slice spring onions, keeping the green tops for garnish.

Mix soy sauce, rice vinegar, sugar, sesame oil and black pepper in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. If the udon are tightly packed, loosen them gently under warm running water for 20–30 seconds, then drain; do not boil fresh udon until soft. Keep the measured 80 ml water beside the pan for stir-frying.

Heat 20 ml neutral oil in a wide non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Add the tofu in one layer and leave it untouched for 2–3 minutes until golden below. Turn and cook another 2 minutes, then lift out onto a plate. Work in two pans or batches if the pan is too small; crowded tofu steams.

Add the remaining 25 ml oil to the pan. Stir-fry onion and carrot for 2 minutes, then mushrooms, cabbage, ginger and the pale spring-onion pieces for 2–3 minutes. The cabbage should wilt but stay a little crisp. Add the udon and measured water, lift and separate gently with tongs, and toss over high heat for 2 minutes until the water evaporates.

Return the tofu to the pan. Pour the sauce against the hot side of the pan, let it sizzle for a few seconds, then toss through the noodles for 1–2 minutes until everything is hot and lightly glossy, with a few toasted noodle edges. Divide among four bowls and scatter the green spring-onion tops over each. Serve immediately.
tips: This is a vegetarian tofu version of Japanese yaki udon; many bottled mentsuyu sauces and bonito garnishes contain fish, so this recipe uses a simple soy-based sauce instead. Handle thick udon gently to avoid breaking them. If using dried udon, cook and drain them according to the packet before stir-frying; 800 g refers to fresh udon.
notes: Quantities serve four adults. Check the doneness cues in each step and adjust seasoning to taste. Jain suitability depends on your household ingredient rules.
